about.title: Egypt and the Indus Valley
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. This class covers two civilizations and two debates (the Indus script and the Indus decline). It is split into about 21 short beats, each with one idea and, in most cases, a check question.

say.text: Welcome back. Last class we met the first cities and the first writing. Today we put two early river civilizations side by side: Egypt and the Indus Valley.

show.text: Two Rivers, Two Civilizations

say.text: First, a term. A river civilization is an early society whose farms and cities grew up beside a great river.

show.text: River civilization

say.text: Take the Nile in Egypt. Every year it flooded, and when the water went down it left a layer of dark, nutrient-rich mud called silt. Farmers could plant in that silt.

show.text: A narrow green strip of farmland along the Nile, with dry desert on both sides.

ask.q: What did the Nile flood leave behind that helped farming?
ask.why: The receding Nile left a brown layer of silt full of nutrients, which allowed farming.

say.text: The Indus people also lived by a river. Their land sat at the dry edge of the monsoon rains, so farming depended heavily on river water.

show.text: Two areas marked. Egypt: the Nile in northeast Africa. Indus: the Indus River in what is now Pakistan and northwest India.

say.text: Now the timing. Egypt was joined into one kingdom first. Indus cities were big by about 2600 BCE, around when Egypt's Great Pyramid was built.

show.text: c. 3150 BCE Egypt unified | by 2600 BCE Indus cities are large | c. 2589–2566 BCE Khufu's reign

say.text: Let's start with Egypt's ruler. The word pharaoh is usually explained as meaning "big house", probably the great palace where the king lived.

show.text: Pharaoh

say.text: Egypt was unified about 3150 BCE under one king. Egyptians believed the pharaoh's divine presence kept justice, peace and good harvests, and the yearly Nile flood was seen as a sign of that.

show.text: One kingdom|One king|Believed divine|Linked to the Nile flood

ask.q: What did ancient Egyptians believe about the pharaoh?
ask.right: He had a divine presence that kept justice, peace and prosperity
wrong: He was an ordinary farmer chosen by lottery
He was a foreign general with no religious role
He had no connection to the Nile
ask.why: The pressbook says Egyptians believed the pharaoh's divine presence kept justice and prosperity, as the annual Nile flooding showed.

say.text: A pharaoh's power showed in stone. The Great Pyramid was the tomb of King Khufu, and it was the largest building in the world up to that time.

show.text: c. 2589–2566 BCE: Khufu's reign (dates vary by source)

ask.q: Who was the Great Pyramid built for?
wrong: Alexander the Great, as a fortress
ask.why: Britannica says it was built as a royal tomb for Khufu, second king of the 4th dynasty.

say.text: Who built it? Not slaves, say historians today. Skilled and unskilled Egyptian workers were paid, and the Nile carried the heavy stone on boats.

show.text: Paid Egyptian workers|Stone moved by boat on the Nile|Granite came from Aswan|Limestone casing came from Tura

ask.q: According to historians today, who built the pyramids?
ask.right: Skilled and unskilled Egyptian workers who were paid
ask.why: World History Encyclopedia says Egyptian workers were compensated, and worker housing has been found at Giza.

say.text: Now the Indus. Egypt is famous for royal tombs. The Indus is famous for something different: its planned cities. We call these people the Harappans, after the city of Harappa.

show.text: Harappan (Indus) civilization

say.text: By 2600 BCE small farming communities had grown into big cities. Archaeologists have found more than 1,052 cities and settlements, mostly along the Indus and its tributaries.

show.text: 1,052+ cities and settlements found

ask.q: About how many Indus cities and settlements have been found?
ask.why: More than 1,052 cities and settlements have been found, mainly near the Indus and its tributaries.

say.text: The cities had a plan. A grid means straight streets that cross each other at right angles, like a chessboard. Mohenjo-daro had a raised citadel to the west and a grid-patterned lower city to the east.

show.text: A bird's-eye drawing of a city: a raised walled area on the west side, and rows of houses on straight crossing streets to the east.

ask.q: What is a grid street plan?
ask.right: Straight streets that cross at right angles
wrong: Streets built only along the river
ask.why: Britannica says the lower city of Indus towns was laid out in a grid pattern of streets.

say.text: Bricks, weights and seals were also made in standard sizes across the Indus lands. That sameness suggests some kind of authority was regulating them.

show.text: Standardization

ask.q: What does the sameness of Indus bricks and weights suggest?
ask.right: Some authority or governance regulated them
wrong: Every town copied by pure accident
The bricks were all made in one workshop
ask.why: The uniform bricks, weights and seals suggest some form of authority and governance.

say.text: Cities need clean water and a way to remove waste. Indus streets had covered drains of baked brick, connected to household bathing areas and latrines.

show.text: A street in cross-section: a covered brick drain running under the road, with small channels leading from houses.

ask.q: Where did household waste water go in Harappan cities?
ask.right: Into covered brick drains along the streets
ask.why: Streets had covered drains of baked bricks linked to household bathing areas and latrines.

say.text: So we can compare. Egypt: one divine king, a huge royal tomb. Indus: planned cities, but no agreed palace or royal tomb. Sources differ even on whether the Indus had monumental buildings.

show.text: EGYPT: Nile floods | one divine pharaoh | pyramid tombs ||| INDUS: river floods and monsoon | grid cities, drains, standard bricks | no clear ruler, palace or temple identified

ask.q: Which describes the Indus cities better?
ask.right: Planned grid streets and drains, with no clear palace or royal tomb identified
wrong: Tents that moved with the seasons
ask.why: The sources describe planned streets and drainage. One source says there is no evidence of monuments, palaces or temples, and another mentions monumental architecture, so the evidence is debated.

say.text: Next, trade. Mesopotamian texts name a distant land, Meluhha. Most scholars link Meluhha to the Indus. Indus seals, beads and pottery turn up in Mesopotamia. Carnelian beads made in the Indus were found in Queen Puabi's tomb at Ur.

show.text: An arrow from the Indus region by sea to Mesopotamia, passing the Persian Gulf.

ask.q: Which Indus-made stone beads were probably found in a Mesopotamian queen's tomb?
ask.why: The cloak of beads from Queen Puabi's tomb at Ur is probably made largely of Indian beads, particularly carnelian.

say.text: The Indus people also used signs, about 400 of them. Most are on small stamp seals, probably used in trade. Nobody can read them yet.

show.text: Indus script (undeciphered)

say.text: Why not? The inscriptions are very short, and no bilingual text has been found. A bilingual text is the same message in a known language beside the unknown one. Over a hundred attempts have been published, and none is widely accepted.

show.text: About 400 signs|Very short inscriptions|No bilingual text|100+ attempts, none accepted

ask.q: Why is the Indus script still unread?
ask.right: The inscriptions are very short and there is no bilingual text
wrong: Scholars all agree it is just decoration
It is written in modern English
ask.why: Britannica names brevity of inscriptions and lack of bilingual inscriptions.

say.text: Experts disagree about what the script is. Some propose a Dravidian language, some an Indo-Aryan one. Others think it may not be a full writing system at all.

show.text: A LANGUAGE: Dravidian proposals | Indo-Aryan proposals ||| NOT A FULL LANGUAGE: pictographic signs for a mixed population | maybe not full writing

ask.q: Do scholars agree on what language the Indus script records?
ask.why: Britannica says no decipherment is widely accepted, and links to Egyptian and Sumerian are now mostly considered discredited.

say.text: Now a puzzle: why did the Indus cities decline? One leading idea is climate. From about 2500 BCE the summer monsoon rains gradually dried up, making farming near the cities hard. People moved east toward the Ganges basin.

show.text: Monsoon: seasonal rain-bearing winds

ask.q: What is the leading climate idea about the Indus decline?
ask.right: Monsoon rains weakened, so farming near the cities got harder
wrong: Rain became too heavy every year
ask.why: WHOI researchers found that from about 2500 BCE the summer monsoon gradually dried up, and people moved east.

say.text: It wasn't overnight. A 2025 study found repeated droughts, each over 85 years long. Smaller settlements kept going, spread out to new places. The big-city era lasted about 700 years, versus about 430 for Egypt's Old Kingdom.

show.text: Years covered by the periods in this class

ask.right: No, the decline was gradual and smaller settlements continued
wrong: Yes, everyone disappeared in one day
Yes, a pyramid fell on the cities
Yes, the river turned into a lake
ask.why: Researchers describe a gradual decline, and evidence suggests small settlements continued, dispersed to other areas.

say.text: Not everyone agrees on the cause. An older theory blamed invaders called Aryans. Many scholars now favor climate. Others point to river shifts or floods, and some say the timing of climate change and collapse is still debated.

show.text: MANY NOW: climate change, repeated droughts ||| OTHERS: river shifts or floods | older invasion theory | debate over timing

ask.q: Why are some experts careful about blaming climate alone?
ask.right: Timing is debated and other factors such as river shifts may have mattered
wrong: Because there was never any monsoon
Because the Indus had no rivers
Because the cities are still occupied
ask.why: One study notes controversy about how closely climate change and collapse lined up, and another says climate alone was probably not the cause.

say.text: Frame of reference. Around 2500 BCE, Khufu's pyramid was being built in Egypt and Indus cities were large. In England, Stonehenge's biggest stones were raised. Sargon of Akkad ruled Mesopotamia from 2334 to 2279 BCE.

show.text: c. 2589–2566 BCE Khufu | c. 2500 BCE Stonehenge sarsens raised | 2334–2279 BCE Sargon of Akkad | 2181 BCE Old Kingdom ends

ask.q: What was being raised in England around 2500 BCE?
ask.why: The British Museum says the larger sarsen stones were raised around 2500 BC.

say.text: To wrap up: both civilizations grew up beside rivers, but they looked different. Egypt had a divine king and pyramids. The Indus had planned cities and an unread script. Next class, we look at the wider Bronze Age world and its collapse.

show.text: Rivers fed farms|Egypt: pharaohs and pyramids|Indus: planned cities, trade, unread script|Indus decline: gradual, debated

ask.q: What did Egypt and the Indus have in common?
ask.right: Both grew along rivers whose water supported farming
wrong: Both used the same readable script
Both ended in a single day
ask.why: Egypt relied on the Nile flood and silt, and the Indus relied on river water for farming.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The Great Pyramid is built for Khufu in Egypt, and the Indus cities are large urban centers.
The large sarsen stones of Stonehenge in England are raised.
Sargon of Akkad rules and builds the first Mesopotamian empire; his empire ends around 2154 BCE.
Egypt's Old Kingdom ends, while the Indus people are slowly shifting east as the monsoon weakens.

other_side.claim: The Indus script is a true writing system for a spoken language.
other_side.other_view: Some scholars argue the signs may not be a fully developed writing system, and others propose a pictographic system meant for a mixed-language population. Proposals for the language include Dravidian and Indo-Aryan, and none is widely accepted.

other_side.claim: Climate change (weakening monsoons and droughts) was a key cause of the Indus decline.
other_side.other_view: An older theory blamed Aryan invaders. Some experts stress river changes or a great flood. One study says controversy remains about how closely climate change and collapse lined up, and another says climate alone was probably not the cause.

other_side.claim: A central authority governed the Indus cities, because bricks, weights and seals are so uniform.
other_side.other_view: Archaeological records give no clear center of authority or images of rulers, and one source finds no evidence of palaces or temples. Britannica does describe monumental architecture, so sources differ.

other_side.claim: Khufu reigned c. 2589–2566 BCE and the Great Pyramid was built in that time.
other_side.other_view: Dates differ by source. Britannica places Khufu's 4th dynasty at about 2543–2436 BCE and says the pyramid was completed in the early 25th century BCE. Other sources give around 2560 or 2600 BCE.
Historians today say Egyptian workers, skilled and unskilled, were paid. Worker towns and overseers' homes have been found at Giza.
